prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · Plan comparison (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Feature" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 83px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 79px
  col 3: header "Pro" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 4: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 229px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 419px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"bad","why":"Squeezes all five columns into 360px, splitting headers and values into fragments such as 'Featur e', 'Enterp rise', 'Unlimit ed', 'Custo m' and 'Comm unity'; the table fits but is hard to scan and compare."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"The four plan columns stay intact and readable, with Free/Pro/Enterprise in a sensible progression; Notes is pushed off-screen, but the visible primary comparison works well."},"C":{"grade":"good","why":"Best balance of the visible columns: Feature, Free and Pro are intact, Enterprise gets enough width for its longer values, and the plan columns fit the 360px frame; Notes remains off-screen but scrollable."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Primary columns are readable and unsplit, but Enterprise is over-wide and the first four columns already slightly exceed the available width, adding unnecessary horizontal scroll while Notes remains off-screen."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Similar to D with a wider Feature and narrower Enterprise; readable, but still slightly overflows and gives no clear advantage over C."},"F":{"grade":"poor","why":"Enterprise is excessively wide, creating large empty areas and forcing a larger horizontal scroll while Notes disappears completely; the three-line support value does not justify the lost width."}},"best":["C"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"The full width and readability of the off-screen Notes column cannot be verified from the screenshots; row heights suggest it remains narrow in every layout, which affects the overall judgment."}
